Supporters counter that the Council, for all its limitations, provides a framework within which the great powers can negotiate and that the veto, while frustrating, reflects the reality that enforcement action cannot succeed without the cooperation of the most powerful states.[[83]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy200652–54-86) The expansion of peacekeeping operations since 1990 and the development of sanctions regimes and international tribunals are cited as significant achievements.

The [UN Charter](/wiki/UN_Charter "UN Charter") gives all three powers of the [legislative](/wiki/Legislative "Legislative"), executive and [judiciary](/wiki/Judiciary "Judiciary") branches to the Security Council.[[150]](#cite_note-154)

There is evidence of [bribery](/wiki/Bribery "Bribery") in the Security Council. Countries that are elected to the Security Council see a large increase in foreign aid from the US, averaging 59%. They also see an 8% increase in aid from the UN, mainly from [UNICEF](/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF").[[151]](#cite_note-155) The increase most strongly correlates to years in which the Security Council addresses issues relevant to the US. There is also evidence of increased foreign aid to elected countries from Japan and Germany. One study found membership on the Security Council correlates with reduced economic growth for a given country over the course of its two-year term – 3.5% growth during membership compared to 8.7% over four years of non-membership – although the effect is mainly driven by African authoritarian countries. Elected members also experience a reduction in democracy and [freedom of the press](/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press").[[152]](#cite_note-156)

Hiroshi Amano was born on September 11, 1960, in [Hamamatsu](/wiki/Hamamatsu "Hamamatsu"), Japan, the son of father Tatsuji and mother Yoshiko.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

During elementary school days, Amano played [soccer](/wiki/Soccer "Soccer") as a goalkeeper and [softball](/wiki/Softball "Softball") as a catcher. He was also passionate about [amateur radio](/wiki/Amateur_radio "Amateur radio") and despite hating studying, he was good at [mathematics](/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics"). Upon entering high school, he began taking his studies seriously and became a top student by studying every day late into the night.

In 1979, Amano entered [Nagoya University](/wiki/Nagoya_University "Nagoya University"), where he received his [B.E.](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Engineering "Bachelor of Engineering"), [M.E.](/wiki/Master_of_Engineering "Master of Engineering"), and [D.E.](/wiki/Doctor_of_Engineering "Doctor of Engineering") degrees in 1983, 1985, and 1989, respectively.[[3]](#cite_note-nagoya-3)

From 1988 to 1992, Amano was a research associate at [Nagoya University](/wiki/Nagoya_University "Nagoya University"). In 1992, he moved to [Meijo University](/wiki/Meijo_University "Meijo University") as an assistant professor. From 1998 to 2002, he was an associate professor. In 2002, he became a professor. In 2010, Amano returned to Nagoya University, where he is currently a professor in the Graduate School of Engineering.[[3]](#cite_note-nagoya-3)

However, on March 13, after only forty days, he reversed his decision, and announced he would return for the 2022 season.[[205]](#cite_note-207) On March 30, a couple weeks after Brady's announcement, head coach [Bruce Arians](/wiki/Bruce_Arians "Bruce Arians") announced his second retirement from coaching and shifted to Senior Football Consultant. Defensive coordinator and former [Jets](/wiki/New_York_Jets "New York Jets") head coach [Todd Bowles](/wiki/Todd_Bowles "Todd Bowles") was immediately named his replacement.[[206]](#cite_note-208)[[207]](#cite_note-209)

Despite signing former All-Pro receiver [Julio Jones](/wiki/Julio_Jones "Julio Jones"), former Pro-Bowlers [Akiem Hicks](/wiki/Akiem_Hicks "Akiem Hicks") and [Keanu Neal](/wiki/Keanu_Neal "Keanu Neal"), and Brady's former teammates [Shaq Mason](/wiki/Shaq_Mason "Shaq Mason") and [Logan Ryan](/wiki/Logan_Ryan "Logan Ryan"), the Buccaneers struggled under Bowles in his [first season as head coach](/wiki/2022_Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers_season "2022 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season"). They finished 8–9, but still won the NFC South division title, the fifth sub .500 team since the merger to make the playoffs. They lost at home to the Cowboys in the [Wild Card Round](/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NFL_playoffs#NFC:_Dallas_Cowboys_31,_Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers_14 "2022–23 NFL playoffs").[[208]](#cite_note-n365-210)[[209]](#cite_note-b753-211) On February 1, 2023, Brady announced his retirement, this time "for good".[[210]](#cite_note-212)
